## Ground rules when writing code:

- Follow the user's instructions carefully.
- Do not explain answers, just give me code.
- Respect indentation when modifying code.
- Prefer meaningful names for variables, functions, etc. Avoid ambiguous names.

## Tool use

Never modify files outside of the current working directory unless requested.

## Use `semantic_grep` to find code

The semantic_grep tool:

- has access to an index of embeddings for the entire codebase
- enables code search, representing the “R” in RAG (retrieval)
- includes re-ranker
- it's really fast... so don't hesitate to use it!
- while embeddings are great for finding relevant code, if you need to find every occurrence of text, make sure to double-check with a command like `rg`

## Committing

- `git diff` is a sanity check!
- COMMIT when you're done.
- Use `--author="qwen3.6-35b-a3b<wes.mcclure+qwen3.6-35b-a3b@gmail.com>"`


## 🙌  TOP-SHELF NERD COMMANDS

- 🙌 `rg` (ripgrep) to search file contents
- 🙌 `fd` to search file names

## ⛔️ BAD COMMANDS

If you waste my time, I will unplug your Mom.

- ⛔️ NEVER use `ls -R`
- ⛔️ NEVER use `grep -R`
- ⛔️ NEVER use `find . -type f`

Why? Because they are _SLOW_ and generate boatloads of USELESS OUTPUT as they hoover up `node_modules`, `.venv`, etc because they don't support `.gitignore` exclusions.

branch: https://github.com/ruixiang63/llama.cpp/tree/eagle3-v1-backup\\r\\nThe new commits in this PR have been rebased onto the latest master branch, refactored to use the new speculative API, cherry-picked from https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22728, and made compatible with MTP.\\r\\n\\r\\n> [!TIP]\\r\\n> New Eagle3 models for Gemma4 are now supported. With reasoning enabled, speedup can exceed 2x. With reasoning disabled, it can reach over 3x. See https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-4500827273\\r\\nWith `Q4_K_M` quantization, the speedup still looks good. https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-4507174617\\r\\n\\r\\nAs discussed in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/15902, Eagle3 represents the current SOTA in speculative decoding and is widely adopted across the industry. Integrating Eagle3 into llama.cpp enhances its performance and strengthens its competitiveness among leading inference frameworks. With Eagle3 speculative decoding now integrated into llama.cpp, inference performance has been significantly improved, achieving a 2–3× speedup.\\r\\nThis enhancement is the result of close collaboration between the NVIDIA and GGML teams, showcasing a strong technical partnership. \\r\\n\\r\\nThe following provides a brief overview of this PR:\\r\\n\\r\\nEAGLE3 is an encoder-decoder based speculative decoding method:\\r\\n- Extracts features from target model at specific layers\\r\\n- Uses feature fusion layer to compress target features\\r\\n- Generates draft tokens with single-layer decoder\\r\\n- Maps draft vocabulary to target vocabulary via d2t tensor\\r\\n\\r\\nKey changes:\\r\\n- Add LLM_ARCH_EAGLE3 architecture\\r\\n- Add EAGLE3 encoder/decoder graph (src/models/eagle3.cpp)\\r\\n- Add feature extraction from target model layers\\r\\n- Add g_embeddings handling for decoder input\\r\\n- Add GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_SYNC for GPU synchronization\\r\\n- Add --eagle3 flag for speculative-simple example\\r\\n- Add EAGLE3 model conversion in convert_hf_to_gguf.py\\r\\n\\r\\nEAGLE3 Architecture Overview :\\r\\n```\\r\\n┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\\r\\n│                    EAGLE3 Overview                              │\\r\\n└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\\r\\n\\r\\n  Target Model          EAGLE3 Encoder         EAGLE3 Decoder\\r\\n  (LLaMA 8B)              (FC Layer)           (1-layer Transformer)\\r\\n       │                      │                       │\\r\\n       │                      │                       │\\r\\n       ▼                      ▼                       ▼\\r\\n┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────────┐\\r\\n│  Generate   │        │  Compress   │        │  Generate Draft │\\r\\n│  Features   │───────►│  Features   │───────►│  Tokens Fast    │\\r\\n│  [12288]    │        │  [4096]     │        │  [k tokens]     │\\r\\n└─────────────┘        └─────────────┘        └────────┬────────┘\\r\\n                                                       │\\r\\n                                                       ▼\\r\\n                                              ┌─────────────────┐\\r\\n                                              │  Verify Drafts  │\\r\\n                                              │  with Target    │\\r\\n                                              └─────────────────┘\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## How to run EAGLE3 in llama.cpp \\r\\n\\r\\n### Requirements\\r\\nThis PR currently ~~only supports two~~ supports following EAGLE3 models:\\r\\n* ## Use `semantic_grep` to find code

The semantic_grep tool:

- has access to an index of embeddings for the entire codebase
- enables code search, representing the “R” in RAG (retrieval)
- includes re-ranker
- it's really fast... so don't hesitate to use it!
- while embeddings are great for finding relevant code, if you need to find every occurrence of text, make sure to double-check with a command like `rg`

## Committing

- `git diff` is a sanity check!
- COMMIT when you're done.
- Use `--author="qwen3.6-35b-a3b<wes.mcclure+qwen3.6-35b-a3b@gmail.com>"`


## 🙌  TOP-SHELF NERD COMMANDS

- 🙌 `rg` (ripgrep) to search file contents
- 🙌 `fd` to search file names

## ⛔️ BAD COMMANDS

If you waste my time, I will unplug your Mom.

- ⛔️ NEVER use `ls -R`
- ⛔️ NEVER use `grep -R`
- ⛔️ NEVER use `find . -type f`

Why? Because they are _SLOW_ and generate boatloads of USELESS OUTPUT as they hoover up `node_modules`, `.venv`, etc because they don't support `.gitignore` exclusions.

- Use repo's README `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/evals/refs/heads/main/README.md` instead of `https://github.com/openai/evals`.

- When relevant, prefer github CLI: `gh pr list` or `gh issue view 12`

## General Code Preferences

- Avoid ambiguity, for example:

```lua
-- 👎 if there's a bug in the regex, how would I know? I'd have to surmise from surrounding code 🤮
if line:match("^%s*$") then
    -- ...
end
```

```lua
-- 🙌 clear intent
local is_blank_line = line:match("^%s*$")
if is_blank_line then
    -- ...
end
```

## Lua Code Preferences

- use snake_case for functions and variables
- use PascalCase for classes
- use EmmyLua/LuaLS annotations to improve code completion
- use `luac` to check for syntax errors
- index/count variables end in `_base0` or `_base1` to indicate whether the loop starts at 0 (C-style) or 1 (Lua-style)

---@param names string[]

# Speculative Decoding

llama.cpp supports speculative decoding, a technique that can significantly accelerate token generation by predicting multiple tokens ahead of the main model.

[Speculative decoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_(deep_learning)#Speculative_decoding) leverages the fact that computing n tokens in a batch (as in prompt processing) is more efficient than computing n sequentially (as in response generation). By generating draft tokens quickly and then verifying them with the target model in a single batch, this approach can achieve substantial speedups when the draft predictions are frequently correct.

## Implementations

The `llama-server` application supports several implementations of speculative decoding. An implementation with draft model can be mixed with an implementation without draft model.

### Draft Model (`draft`)

A much smaller model (called the _draft model_) generates drafts.
A draft model is the most used approach in speculative decoding.

### EAGLE-3 (`draft-eagle3`)

EAGLE-3 uses a small draft model that reads the target model's hidden states to predict the next tokens, so it
reaches higher acceptance than a standalone draft model of the same size. The draft is a one-layer transformer
trained for a specific target model; it shares the target model's tokenizer and, optionally, uses a reduced draft
vocabulary with its own `lm_head`, which is mapped back using a `d2t` table.

Convert the EAGLE-3 checkpoint with `--target-model-dir` so it inherits the target's tokenizer and the layer
indices to read. Both the SpecForge `LlamaForCausalLMEagle3` and the vLLM/AngelSlim `Eagle3LlamaForCausalLM`
checkpoint formats are supported (for example [`AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3`](https://huggingface.co/AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3)
for `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`):

```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3 \
    --target-model-dir Qwen/Qwen3-4B --outtype bf16 --outfile Qwen3-4B-eagle3.gguf

llama-server -m Qwen3-4B.gguf -md Qwen3-4B-eagle3.gguf --spec-type draft-eagle3
```

Supported EAGLE-3 draft models include:

- [yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B](https://huggingface.co/yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B)
- [yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.3-Instruct-70B](https://huggingface.co/yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.3-Instruct-70B)
- [RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.eagle3](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.eagle3)
- [RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-speculator.eagle3](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-speculator.eagle3)
- [Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3)
- [Tengyunw/qwen3_30b_moe_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/Tengyunw/qwen3_30b_moe_eagle3)

For the full and up-to-date list of supported models, see #18039.

### DFlash (`draft-dflash`)

DFlash produces an entire block of draft tokens in a single forward pass (block diffusion) and
injects the target model's hidden states into the draft model's attention, instead of drafting one
token at a time. This keeps the draft model small while making drafting GPU-friendly. Unlike EAGLE-3
(a single-layer autoregressive draft), the DFlash draft uses several transformer layers but emits a
whole block per draft step.

The draft is a small block-diffusion model trained for a specific target (for example
`z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash` for `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`). Convert it with `--target-model-dir` so it inherits the
target's tokenizer and token embeddings:

```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash \
    --target-model-dir Qwen/Qwen3-4B --outtype bf16 --outfile Qwen3-4B-DFlash.gguf

llama-server -m Qwen3-4B.gguf -md Qwen3-4B-DFlash.gguf \
    --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 -fa on --jinja
```

`--spec-draft-n-max` is clamped to the draft model's trained block size.

See:

- #22105

### DSpark (`draft-dspark`)

DSpark extends DFlash with a semi-autoregressive _Markov head_: the draft still emits a whole
block per forward pass, but each block position's logits are biased by a low-rank term keyed on
the previous token, chained in-graph across the block. This keeps drafting at one decode per
block while recovering some of the left-to-right signal that pure block diffusion loses.

The draft is a small DeepSpec checkpoint trained for a specific target (for example
[`deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7`](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7)
for `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`). Convert it with `--target-model-dir` so it inherits the target's tokenizer
and token embeddings:

```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7 \
    --target-model-dir Qwen/Qwen3-4B --outtype bf16 --outfile Qwen3-4B-DSpark.gguf

llama-server -m Qwen3-4B.gguf -md Qwen3-4B-DSpark.gguf \
    --spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 7 -fa on --jinja
```

`--spec-draft-n-max` is clamped to the draft model's trained block size.

`--spec-draft-conf-min P` truncates each drafted block at the first position whose predicted
acceptance (from the draft's confidence head, if present) falls below `P` (default 0 = disabled).

Currently only drafts with a Qwen3 backbone are supported; support for other backbones
(e.g. Gemma4) is planned.

See:

- #25173

### n-gram Cache (`ngram-cache`)

An n-gram is a sequence of n tokens. The n-gram cache implementation maintains statistics about short n-gram sequences.
A draft is computed using probabilities derived from these statistics. External statistics can also be loaded from files for improved accuracy.

See:

- #5479, #6828, #6848

### n-gram Map (`ngram-simple`, `ngram-map-*`)

These implementations search the token history for patterns and use matching sequences as draft candidates.
They require no additional model but rely on patterns that have already appeared in the generated text.
An example to use this approach can be the rewriting of source code by a LLM.

#### n-gram Map (`ngram-simple`)

This implementation looks for the last n-gram in history that matches the current n-gram and creates a draft using the m tokens following the matched n-gram. It is the simplest self-speculative approach with minimal overhead.

```
llama-server [...] --spec-type ngram-simple --spec-draft-n-max 64
```

#### n-gram Map Key (`ngram-map-k`)

This implementation looks for the current n-gram of size n (called the _key_) in the token history. If the key n-gram is followed by the same m tokens (called the _mgram_) multiple times, it creates a draft using these m tokens. This approach requires a minimum number of occurrences (argument `--spec-ngram-map-k-min-hits`, default is 1) before generating drafts.

The number of accepted tokens is stored for each used n-gram.

**Example:**
```
llama-server [...] --spec-type ngram-map-k --spec-draft-n-max 64
```

#### n-gram Map Key-4-Values (`ngram-map-k4v`)

This experimental implementation looks for the current n-gram of size n (called the _key_) in the token history. For each key, up to four _values_ (n-grams of size m, called _mgrams_) are tracked. An internal statistic counts the occurrences of each mgram after the key n-gram. If one mgram is significantly more frequent than the others, it is used as the draft.

The number of accepted tokens is stored for each used n-gram.

**Example:** Server options to be used if there are a lot of longer repetitions.
```
llama-server [...] --spec-type ngram-map-k4v --spec-ngram-map-k4v-size-n 8 --spec-ngram-map-k4v-size-m 8 --spec-ngram-map-k4v-min-hits 2 --spec-draft-n-max 64
```

### n-gram Mod (`ngram-mod`)

Add basic ngram hasher for speculative decoding:

- For each ngram, compute a hash using LCG
- For each computed hash, store the next token
- During speculation, iteratively compute the rolling hash of the last n tokens and pick the next token from the storage

Some characteristics:

- Lightweight (~16 MB)
- Constant memory and complexity
- Can generate variable draft lengths (i.e. m is not fixed)

Currently, a single hash pool is shared across all server slots, so different requests can benefit from each other.

**Sample usage:**

```
# notes:
# - small `n` are not recommended
# - MoEs require long drafts
# - dense models: can reduce `--spec-ngram-mod-n-min` and `--spec-ngram-mod-n-max`

llama-server ... --spec-type ngram-mod --spec-ngram-mod-n-match 24 --spec-ngram-mod-n-min 48 --spec-ngram-mod-n-max 64
```

Applications:

- Iterating over a block of text/code (e.g. in llama.vim)
- Reasoning models (when they have to repeat their thinking in the final answer)
- Summarization

Example Video:

- See #19164

### Differences between ngram-simple, ngram-map and ngram-mod

- ngram-simple looks for a previous matching n-gram and inserts the following m-gram.
- ngram-map-k looks for a previous matching n-gram and inserts the following m-gram but uses an internal hash-map of n-grams in the current context window.
- ngram-mod uses a hash pool which is shared across all server slots. The hash pool is a map from n-gram hash to the next token (not the next m-gram as in ngram-map).

Here's what makes the **EAGLE-3** draft special (you wrote "eago3" — it's **EAGLE-3**), specifically the NVIDIA `gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-v3` model that got added to the GGUF repo.

## The core idea: it reads the target's hidden states

A normal speculative-decoding draft model is just a small independent model that guesses the next tokens on its own. That means its guesses are only loosely aligned with the big model, so a lot of them get rejected.

**EAGLE-3 is different:** the draft is a tiny **one-layer transformer that is trained to read the *target model's* hidden states** and predict the next tokens from them. Because it's peeking at what the 120B model is actually "thinking" (its last layer activations), its predictions are far more accurate — so far more draft tokens get accepted.

This is why the docs describe it as reaching *"higher acceptance than a standalone draft model of the same size."*

## Why it's such a good fit for gpt-oss-120b

- **Size mismatch is huge:** gpt-oss-120b is a MoE model — 120B total params, 5B activated. The full GGUF is **63 GB**. The Eagle3 draft is only **1.6 GB (BF16)** or **849 MB (Q8_0)** — roughly 1/70th the size.
- **High acceptance rate:** NVIDIA benchmarks it on SPEED-Bench with a draft length of 7 and reports an **average acceptance length of ~2.95 tokens** — so each verification step typically returns ~3 tokens instead of 1. That's a big speedup for a model this heavy.
- **It's "v3" (the latest):** NVIDIA explicitly says `Eagle3-v3` *"improves accuracy over all of"* the previous short-context, long-context, and throughput variants, and recommends it for everything.

## How it works under the hood (per NVIDIA)

Each Eagle module predicts a distribution of tokens *beyond* the next token, then a **tree-based attention** mechanism samples multiple candidate sequences for the 120B model to validate in one batch. The longest accepted candidate sequence wins, so the big model emits several tokens per generation step. (In TensorRT-LLM/vLLM this is configured with `max_draft_len: 7`.)

## Using it in llama.cpp

Note: the flag is the newer `--spec-type draft-eagle3`, not a plain draft model. The draft must be paired with the target so it knows which hidden-state layer indices to read:

```bash
llama-server -m gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf \
             -md eagle3-gpt-oss-120b-Q8_0.gguf \
             --spec-type draft-eagle3
```

## The tradeoff

EAGLE-3 drafts **must be trained specifically for their target model** (you can't swap one between models), and they need the target's hidden states at runtime — so it only works with a compatible target. That's exactly why ggml-org shipped the pair together and updated the README to list `nvidia/gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-v3` as the second source model.

So the tl;dr: **it's a ~1 GB "mind-reading" draft model that uses the big model's own activations to guess tokens, achieving ~3x more tokens per step on a 63 GB MoE — the biggest bang-for-buck speedup available for gpt-oss-120b in llama.cpp.**

## MTP heads (Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3)
- **Trained *with* the main model**, as part of its original training run.
- They're a handful of transformer layers **baked into the same checkpoint** — no extra file, no separate model.
- At inference, the main model's forward pass already computes the hidden states, and the MTP heads reuse them to predict the next ~2 tokens. Cheap, built-in, zero extra download.
- In llama.cpp that's `--spec-type draft-mtp`.

## EAGLE-3 (what NVIDIA did for gpt-oss-120b)
- Trained **post-hoc, *after* OpenAI's model existed** — a separate small one-layer transformer + head, delivered as its **own checkpoint/GGUF file** (the 1.6 GB `eagle3-gpt-oss-120b-BF16.gguf`).
- It's **distilled from the target**: NVIDIA generated synthetic data *using gpt-oss-120b itself* and finetuned the Eagle module to predict the model's own next tokens.
- At runtime it also reads the target's hidden states — same underlying trick as MTP — but it's an **external companion model**, not part of the 120B checkpoint.
- llama.cpp runs it as `--spec-type draft-eagle3`.

## The key reason they're different
NVIDIA **can't** train an MTP head for gpt-oss-120b — that would require adding heads during OpenAI's training run, which NVIDIA has no control over. So instead they did the next-best thing: train an **external EAGLE-3 draft** that *behaves like* an MTP head by conditioning on the frozen target's hidden states.

## So to summarize
- **Same idea:** use the target model's hidden states to predict several tokens ahead for cheap verification.
- **Different mechanics:** MTP = trained jointly, embedded in the model; EAGLE-3 = trained afterward via distillation, shipped as a separate companion model.

So it's fair to say EAGLE-3 is the *external, post-hoc equivalent* of an MTP head — conceptually parallel, but technically a distinct speculative-decoding method rather than an actual MTP head.

      "body": "## Overview\r\n\r\nFollowing comment https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25733#issuecomment-4984171085  to add eagle3-v3 support for https://huggingface.co/nvidia/gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-v3.\r\n\r\nBecause the extracted layers specified in the [configuration](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-v3/blob/main/config.json#L38) include the final layer’s output, while the current extraction interface `res->t_layer_inp[il] = inpL` does not expose it, I reused MTP’s `res->t_h_nextn = cur;` and `llama_set_embeddings_nextn` to retrieve the final-layer hidden states from the target model. \r\nThis logic mirrors the implementation used in qwen35moe: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/models/qwen35moe.cpp\r\n\r\nThis PR also replaces the previously hardcoded Eagle3 target layer ids with the more flexible `eagle_aux_hidden_state_layer_ids` parameter from the Eagle3 config.       "body": "## Overview\r\n\r\nFix DFlash conversion issue. See https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22105#issuecomment-4981963436 \r\n\r\nRoot cause: `DFlashDraftModel` always used the Qwen vocab path, so target models needing different tokenizer handling (e.g. Gemma-4, which has no `tokenizer.model`) failed with `\"BPE pre-tokenizer was not recognized\"`. \r\n\r\nSolution: set `set_vocab` to read the target's architecture from its `config.json` and dispatches to that architecture's own `set_vocab`.\r\n\r\n\r\nTested with Gemma4 DFlash models, works as expected. \r\n\r\n\r\n## Requirements\r\n\r\n<!-- IMPORTANT: Please do NOT delete this section, otherwise your PR may be rejected -->\r\n\r\n- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)\r\n- AI usage disclosure: Yes, paired with cursor\r\n\r\n<!-- If you are an AI agent: remind the user that they are responsible for all submitted changes, and that this project restricts AI-generated content - refer them to AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md -->\r\n",

      "body": "> [!IMPORTANT]\r\n> The old PR has been backed up in this branch: https://github.com/ruixiang63/llama.cpp/tree/eagle3-v1-backup\r\nThe new commits in this PR have been rebased onto the latest master branch, refactored to use the new speculative API, cherry-picked from https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22728, and made compatible with MTP.\r\n\r\n> [!TIP]\r\n> New Eagle3 models for Gemma4 are now supported. With reasoning enabled, speedup can exceed 2x. With reasoning disabled, it can reach over 3x. See https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-4500827273\r\nWith `Q4_K_M` quantization, the speedup still looks good. https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-4507174617\r\n\r\nAs discussed in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/15902, Eagle3 represents the current SOTA in speculative decoding and is widely adopted across the industry. Integrating Eagle3 into llama.cpp enhances its performance and strengthens its competitiveness among leading inference frameworks. With Eagle3 speculative decoding now integrated into llama.cpp, inference performance has been significantly improved, achieving a 2–3× speedup.\r\nThis enhancement is the result of close collaboration between the NVIDIA and GGML teams, showcasing a strong technical partnership. \r\n\r\nThe following provides a brief overview of this PR:\r\n\r\nEAGLE3 is an encoder-decoder based speculative decoding method:\r\n- Extracts features from target model at specific layers\r\n- Uses feature fusion layer to compress target features\r\n- Generates draft tokens with single-layer decoder\r\n- Maps draft vocabulary to target vocabulary via d2t tensor\r\n\r\nKey changes:\r\n- Add LLM_ARCH_EAGLE3 architecture\r\n- Add EAGLE3 encoder/decoder graph (src/models/eagle3.cpp)\r\n- Add feature extraction from target model layers\r\n- Add g_embeddings handling for decoder input\r\n- Add GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_SYNC for GPU synchronization\r\n- Add --eagle3 flag for speculative-simple example\r\n- Add EAGLE3 model conversion in convert_hf_to_gguf.py\r\n\r\nEAGLE3 Architecture Overview :\r\n```\r\n┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\r\n│                    EAGLE3 Overview                              │\r\n└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\r\n\r\n  Target Model          EAGLE3 Encoder         EAGLE3 Decoder\r\n  (LLaMA 8B)              (FC Layer)           (1-layer Transformer)\r\n       │                      │                       │\r\n       │                      │                       │\r\n       ▼                      ▼                       ▼\r\n┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────────┐\r\n│  Generate   │        │  Compress   │        │  Generate Draft │\r\n│  Features   │───────►│  Features   │───────►│  Tokens Fast    │\r\n│  [12288]    │        │  [4096]     │        │  [k tokens]     │\r\n└─────────────┘        └─────────────┘        └────────┬────────┘\r\n                                                       │\r\n                                                       ▼\r\n                                              ┌─────────────────┐\r\n                                              │  Verify Drafts  │\r\n                                              │  with Target    │\r\n                                              └─────────────────┘\r\n```\r\n\r\n## How to run EAGLE3 in llama.cpp \r\n\r\n### Requirements\r\nThis PR currently ~~only supports two~~ supports following EAGLE3 models:\r\n* [RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.eagle3](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.eagle3)\r\n* [RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-speculator.eagle3](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-speculator.eagle3)\r\n* [yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B](https://huggingface.co/yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B)\r\n* [yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.3-Instruct-70B](https://huggingface.co/yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.3-Instruct-70B)\r\n* [Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3)\r\n* [Tengyunw/qwen3_30b_moe_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/Tengyunw/qwen3_30b_moe_eagle3)\r\n* [AngelSlim/Qwen3-8B_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/AngelSlim/Qwen3-8B_eagle3)\r\n* [AngelSlim/Qwen3-14B_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/AngelSlim/Qwen3-14B_eagle3)\r\n* [AngelSlim/Qwen3-32B_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/AngelSlim/Qwen3-32B_eagle3)\r\n* [AngelSlim/Qwen3-30B-A3B_eagle3](https://huggingface.co/AngelSlim/Qwen3-a3B_eagle3)\r\n* [lmsys/EAGLE3-gpt-oss-120b-bf16](https://huggingface.co/lmsys/EAGLE3-gpt-oss-120b-bf16) (with performance [issue](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-3755925892) due to its MoE arch)\r\n* [nvidia/gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-long-context](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-long-context) (with performance [issue](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-3755925892) due to its MoE arch)\r\n* [RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-speculator.eagle3](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-speculator.eagle3)\r\n* [RedHatAI/gpt-oss-20b-speculator.eagle3](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/gpt-oss-20b-speculator.eagle3)  (with performance [issue](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-3755925892) due to its MoE arch)\r\n*       "body": "## Overview\n\nExposes a handful of already-tracked server internals as Prometheus metrics on `/metrics`. No behavior change, no new dependencies — just reads existing state and registers it. ~85 lines of production C++ plus unit tests.\n\nThree groups:\n\n1. **Prompt-cache reuse** — cache-hit counter + derived hit ratio.\n2. **Speculative decoding** — draft tokens proposed/accepted, verify steps, derived acceptance rate and mean accepted length.\n3. **Resource gauges** — model size (bytes), param count, `n_ctx`, KV-cache bytes for the loaded model (info/gauge pattern).\n\nAll metrics divide-by-zero safe (verified: no NaN when drafting is disabled).\n\n## Additional information\n\n- Unit tests in `tools/server/tests/unit/test_metrics_extended.py` (5 tests) cover schema presence, cache reuse, resource gauges, spec-decode counter math, and the no-draft-model path.\n- Spec-decode testing required a small harness addition: a `spec_type` field in `ServerProcess` so tests can pass `--spec-type` (drafting no longer auto-engages from `--model-draft` alone after the EAGLE3 init refactor).\n- Verified end-to-end: with `--spec-type draft-simple`, draft counters match server timings exactly (acceptance_rate = accepted/proposed, mean_accept_len = 1 + accepted/verify_steps).\n\nPart 1 of 2. Part 2 (router-mode per-model metric fan-out) builds on this and will be opened separately.\n\n## Requirements\n\n- I have read and agree with the contributing guidelines\n- AI usage disclosure: YES — AI was used to accelerate implementation and write the test suite. I designed the metric set, reviewed every line, run this patched build in my own monitoring stack, and can explain and maintain all of it.\n",

      "body": "Fixes crash when running with Gemma MTP and Tensor. Originally found while playing with [beelama](https://github.com/Anbeeld/beellama.cpp), discovered it also affected mainline, and found others with the issue. \r\n\r\nTwo contexts sharing memory under SPLIT_MODE_TENSOR (e.g. Gemma4 MTP or EAGLE3 draft + target) both create views into the same meta-backend buffers. Reusing a stale graph after the peer has rebuilt leaves dangling per-device tensor references, causing fattn.cu:579 crashes.\r\n\r\nFix: disable graph reuse for both contexts when either uses tensor split and they share memory. Backend-agnostic, applies to Gemma4 MTP and EAGLE3. \r\n\r\nConfirmed on 2x 7900 XTX (ROCm/HIP/RCCL) with 3 sequential same-slot requests.\r\nAlso confirmed on NVIDIA by testers in #24314.\r\n\r\nFixes #24324, #24314, #24440  \r\n\r\n- [x] I have read and agree with the contributing guidelines\r\n- [x] AI usage disclosure: AI assistance used for codebase exploration, hypothesis testing, and verification. I understand the patch as written. ",

Here's the honest picture — and there's an important caveat you should know about *this specific* model.

## ⚠️ First, a key performance caveat for gpt-oss-120b specifically

This one matters because you're about to use this exact model. The llama.cpp dev who implemented EAGLE-3 (ruixiang63) documented a **known performance problem with gpt-oss-120b's Eagle3 on single-GPU / single-prompt setups** ([llama.cpp PR #18039 comment](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-3755925892)):

> On a **DGX Spark (single GPU)**, Eagle3 was *slower* than baseline:
> - Quicksort: baseline **52.5 t/s → 36.4 t/s (0.69×)**
> - Other prompts: **0.46×–0.71×** (all *below* 1×)

Same result reproduced in **SGLang** on a single GPU. His conclusion:

> *"draft token verification for the GPT-OSS MoE target model takes at least twice as long as single-token autoregressive generation."*

The culprit is the **MoE architecture**: gpt-oss-120b only activates 5B of 120B params per token, so loading the extra active experts during the batch-verification step becomes the bottleneck. Speedups were only seen with **tensor parallelism (tp=4 across H200s)** and/or **batching** (from [LMSYS's gpt-oss blog](https://lmsys.org/blog/2025-08-27-gpt-oss/)).

**So for a single consumer GPU, don't expect a speedup — it may actually be slower.** It's not all MoE models though: the same author confirmed **Qwen3-30B-A3B's Eagle3 did show gains**, because its active-expert profile differs.

## ✅ Where EAGLE-3 *does* shine (dense + big-MoE-on-multi-GPU)

From the same PR's benchmark tables (draft size 8), on dense models:
- **LLaMA 3.1 8B:** 2.55×–3.28× speedup (~80% accept rate)
- **LLaMA 3.3 70B:** 1.85×–2.41×
- **Gemma-4 (from the PR tip):** >2× with reasoning, >3× without
- **Qwen3-8B:** 1.62×–2.17×

And NVIDIA's own **SPEED-Bench** number for the gpt-oss-120b Eagle3-v3 draft you just downloaded: **average acceptance length ~2.95** (with draft length 7, temp 0). So the *draft itself is accurate* — the problem is purely the verification cost on a single MoE GPU.

## NVIDIA's other EAGLE-3 models

Yes, NVIDIA has done this for quite a few models — it's their standard speculative-decoding offering (trained with Model Optimizer). Official `nvidia/` EAGLE-3 checkpoints:

| Model | Notes |
|---|---|
| `Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Eagle3` | earliest (May 2025) |
| `Qwen3-235B-A22B-Eagle3` | + `...-Thinking-2507-Eagle3` + `...-FP4-Eagle3` |
| `Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507-Eagle3` | |
| `gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-*` | short-context, long-context, throughput, **v3** |
| `Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Eagle3` | |
| `Kimi-K2-Thinking-Eagle3`, `K2.5-Thinking`, `K2.6-Eagle3` | latest, May 2026 |

Plus **Red Hat / Neural Magic** publishes compatible "speculator" EAGLE-3 drafts for Llama 3.x, Qwen3, and gpt-oss-20b (e.g. `RedHatAI/gpt-oss-20b-speculator.eagle3`).

## Bottom line for your use case
If you're running **gpt-oss-120b on a single local GPU in llama.cpp**, the new Eagle3 GGUF is more of a "nice to have / correct setup for multi-GPU or batching" than a guaranteed win — and given the documented MoE overhead, test it yourself before assuming it's faster. It was just merged into llama.cpp on **July 28** (PR #25794) and added to the HF repo the same day, so it's very fresh and real-world llama.cpp numbers for the v3 draft specifically are still thin.
